Saurav Bania, Greta Brianti, Jurjan Bootsma, Vincenzo Del Piano, Kobe Degeetere, Andrea Maria, Sergei Solokhin

FCC-ee and the CLD detector

Introduction
  • FCC-ee: a 100 km e⁺e⁻ collider. Four energies: 91 (Z pole), 160 (WW), 240 (ZH), 365 GeV (t̄t).
  • CLD gives us tracking, calorimetry and a 2 T field — enough to reconstruct jets, leptons and missing energy.
  • Each energy hands us several anonymised samples. We don't know what they are yet.
CLD detector — original FCC-ee CLD collaboration deck

Task A: identifying the samples

SM · 160 GeV · step 1 only

Task A: match each anonymous sample to a known process, using cuts on jets, leptons, b-tagging and MET. Two of four samples are identified this way. No excess is searched for at this energy — step 1 of the method is all we need here.

ProcessKey cutsEfficiency
Higgs (ννH, H→bb̄)2 jets b-tag>0.7, 0 leptons, MET cut32.7%*
WW (semileptonic)2 jets, 1 lepton, MET pT>5 GeV43.2%*

* assumed (toy), not measured — the talk gives cuts, not absolute yields.

FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Kobe DegeetereSlide 5

Higgs and WW mass peaks

SM · 160 GeV

Higgs: the dijet mass peaks at ~125 GeV. WW: the effective mass recovers close to √s = 160 GeV, as expected for a semileptonic decay. Both agree with the reported points at the peak.

SM · 365 GeV

t̄t: reconstructed mass sits at the top scale, χ²/ndof = 0.81 — the best agreement in this study. ZZ: dijet mass peaks cleanly at mZ = 91 GeV.

The SM alone doesn't explain it

Evidence · both energies

Sum every identified SM process and compare to the reported points. At both 91 and 365 GeV the excess sits far above that sum. This is why an interpretation is needed — step 2 becomes step 3.

91 GeV
365 GeV
FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Andrea MariaSlide 11

An excess, not an SM sample

BSM · 91 GeV
Excess→Reconstruction→H1: flat bkg→H0: HNL, m≈40→Test

Tight selection: MET pT>3 GeV, ≥1 lepton, small impact parameter. A lepton+jet excess appears. Proposed: a Heavy Neutral Lepton, mass ≈40 GeV. The resonance hypothesis fits better than a flat background: χ²/ndof 4.47 vs. 5.81.

HNL at a Z-factory
FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Andrea MariaSlide 12

An independent cross-check

BSM · 91 GeV

A second, independent variable — missing energy itself — agrees with the same hypothesis: χ²/ndof = 1.14. This isn't the same test twice.

FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Andrea MariaSlide 13

Significance: which definition?

BSM · 91 GeV

The source quotes ~7σ as its headline number. Our background-free recomputation gives 7.9σ — close, but we can't confirm they're the same definition. The source also quotes 5.79σ and 7.8σ elsewhere; we don't know which tier those are (see audit). No look-elsewhere correction is applied: we don't have a real trials count.

Next: Jurjan Bootsma

The excess, and the original method

BSM · 365 GeV

Tighter selection again: low MET, ≥2 jets, ≥2 leptons, Z-veto, b-veto. Original method: hadronic-W channel, one jet assumed, a fixed pairing m(j₂,j₃). The source itself flags this: “sub-optimal pairing might lead to large spread.”

Production and decay, slide 18
FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Jurjan BootsmaSlide 16

CURRENT ANALYSIS Testing the pairing

BSM · 365 GeV

Four jets give three candidate pairings. The fixed original pairing is correct only 33% of the time by construction. Picking the pairing closest to mW instead gets it right 88% of the time, and both peaks narrow sharply. This is evidence the original pairing can mis-associate jets — it supports better reconstruction, not an HNL by itself.

Naive = original · Constrained = current analysis
FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Jurjan BootsmaSlide 17

Resonance vs. SM-tail, and significance

BSM · 365 GeV

Resonance vs. a mis-measured ZZ/WW tail: χ²/ndof 4.12 vs. 215.55 — this specific SM-tail model is disfavoured. Quoted significance: 6.46σ. The background behind that number isn't established in the source.

FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Jurjan BootsmaSlide 18
What has been established -- and what remains open?
Consistency, caveats, and conclusions
Next: Greta Brianti

Open questions

Consistency
  • 40 GeV vs. 150 GeV: two HNL masses. One particle has one mass. This is open, not explained away.
  • 365 GeV background normalisation: not established.
  • No look-elsewhere trial count is available, so none is applied.
  • Every cut efficiency shown is a toy assumption.
  • Rejecting one background model is not proof of an HNL.

Flat vs. resonant hypothesis

Conclusions

At both energies the resonance hypothesis fits better than the flat/SM-tail alternative tested. That supports the interpretation. It doesn't prove it.

91 GeV365 GeV

FCC-ee CLD Collaboration Greta BriantiSlide 22

Where this leaves us

Conclusions

Five SM processes at 365 GeV, two at 160 GeV, each traceable. Two excesses, both consistent with a resonance hypothesis, both with open caveats. FCC-ee's precision lets small, careful excesses be taken seriously — if every claim stays traceable. So: what do you think is really in there?
